title: Solar air heater for a south window or wall
summary: A glazed black box on a south wall or under a south window warms room air while the sun shines: in tests a good 1.2 × 2.4 m (4 × 8 ft) collector with a fan gave about 1 kW at midday, a poor one far less, and all of them nothing at night. Fit a backdraft flap or close it at dusk so it doesn't run backwards. A stalled box gets hot enough to weaken wood and, over months, even ignite it, so nothing that burns touches the absorber.

materials.item: Glazing: clear polycarbonate twinwall (greenhouse or carport panel), about 1.2 × 2.4 m
Or glazing: a storm window, patio door or shower door pane, in a frame
Absorber: window screen (2–3 layers), aluminium cans or downspouts
Sheet metal for brackets and the back lining
Insulation behind the absorber: plain fibreglass or mineral wool (not foam board, not paper-faced)
Flat high-temperature black spray paint (stove, barbecue or engine paint)
Lumber or plywood for the frame, kept off the absorber
Thin plastic film and a light frame for the backdraft flap
12 V fan (computer or car blower fan)
Small solar panel for the fan
Screws, brackets, caulk and foam tape

steps.text: Pick a wall or window facing as close to south as you can, in full sun through the middle of a winter day. For a window box, use a window at least 1.2 m (4 ft) above the ground (Kornher handbook), and not the room's escape window.

Size it: about 1.2 × 2.4 m (4 × 8 ft) is the smallest that does real heating (Reysa pop can test). A passive wall panel bigger than about a fifth of the room's floor area can overheat it (Kornher handbook).
Build a shallow box with an insulated back. Use fibreglass or mineral wool behind the absorber, not foam board (FPL collector), and hold the absorber off any wood on metal brackets with an air gap.
steps.warn: A stalled box passed 93 °C (200 °F) in a USDA test; wood held near 100 °C for months can ignite on its own (FPL collector).

steps.text: Make the absorber: two or more layers of window screen, or cans or downspouts. Paint it flat high-temperature black and let it cure in the sun before closing the box (Reysa pop can test, FPL collector).
steps.warn: Cut can ends by sanding or with snips and gloves; drilling them with a spade bit is dangerous (Reysa pop can test).

steps.text: Cut a low inlet and a high outlet into the room, or fit the box below a window with the window opening as its outlet. Seal every other gap with caulk or foam tape.
Fit a light one-way flap on the room side of the inlet or outlet, or a board you can close at dusk, so it can't run backwards at night (Kornher handbook).

Fit the glazing: polycarbonate twinwall with its UV side out (Palram Sunlite), or a glass pane in a frame. Keep an air gap between the absorber and polycarbonate: Palram rates the sheet to +100 °C for long exposure and +120 °C briefly (Palram guide). Drill a small drain hole at the bottom of the box.
steps.warn: Glass edges cut and big panes are heavy: gloves, and two people for anything door-sized.

steps.text: Optional fan: a 12 V fan on its own small panel, moving about 12–17 L/s per m² of collector (Reysa screen test). Check the panel's open-circuit volts against the fan's rating first.
On the first sunny day, measure the air in and out: expect roughly 17–22 °C warmer passive (Kornher handbook) and up to about 35 °C warmer with a good fan collector (Reysa screen test).
steps.warn: The absorber and glazing get hot enough to burn skin.

steps.text: After dark, hold a strip of tissue at the inlet: if it blows into the room or the room air flows back through the box, close it off or fix the flap.
After the first week, look for peeling paint, warped foam, a film on the glazing or scorched wood, and fix them before you rely on it.
Brush snow off the glazing after storms, and cover the glazing if you won't use it for weeks so it doesn't sit stalled and hot (FPL collector).

notes:
## What it is, and what it isn't

A shallow, insulated box with clear glazing on the front and a black absorber inside, on a south wall or under a south window. Sun heats the absorber; room air passes over it, warms up and goes back into the room, either rising on its own (a window box or thermosiphon air panel) or pushed by a small fan. A well-built collector delivers about half the sunshine that hits it as heat (Kornher handbook). It gives nothing at night or under heavy cloud, and an unguarded one runs backwards after dark.

Passive heaters suit rooms you use by day, and a thermosiphon panel bigger than about a fifth of the room's floor area can overheat the room (Kornher handbook). Fan-driven collectors deliver more heat per square metre than passive ones and can send it further (Kornher handbook).

## Honest numbers from tests

| Collector | Result | Test |
|---|---|---|
| 1.2 × 2.4 m (4 × 8 ft), two layers of aluminium screen, fan | 0.87–1.23 kW (2,980–4,214 Btu/h), 40–43% efficient, air 21–36 °C (38–65 °F) warmer, January, 10–14 °C outside | Reysa screen test |
| Same size, solid back-pass sheet, fan | 36–40% efficient; the screen gave 7–13% more | Reysa screen test |
| Same size, aluminium downspouts, fan | about 0.74 kW against 1.12 kW for the screen beside it | Reysa downspout test |
| 0.6 × 0.9 m (2 × 3 ft), pop cans vs screen, fan | about 0.32 and 0.35 kW in July sun; nearly the same in winter | Reysa pop can test |
| 0.91 m², 96 black soda cans, Nigeria | at best 90 W with a 12 V fan (14% efficient), 130 W passive (16%) | Jidda 2026 |
| Passive window box or wall panel | air leaves about 17–22 °C (30–40 °F) warmer | Kornher handbook |

Reysa's tests are a careful amateur's side-by-side comparisons; he says airflow was hard to measure and the results carry some error (Reysa tests). They were run on sunny days at about 10–14 °C outside, so a Canadian January at −20 °C with a low sun will probably give less. Jidda's is a university test published in an engineering journal. Together they say: a well-built 1.2 × 2.4 m collector with a fan is worth roughly a small electric heater at midday in full sun, a small or poorly matched one gives only a hundred watts or so, and every one gives nothing at night. Reysa reckons 1.2 × 2.4 m is about the smallest that does real heating (Reysa pop can test).

## Which absorber

- **Black screen** (two or more layers of window screen, painted): the best or equal-best in Reysa's tests (Reysa tests), and much quicker to build than cans (Reysa pop can test).
- **Pop cans:** about equal to screen, but cutting, cleaning and gluing hundreds of cans takes far longer; drilling out the can ends with a spade bit is dangerous (Reysa pop can test).
- **Downspouts:** 40–50% behind screen in Reysa's unoptimised test, partly because air flowed unevenly through the tubes (Reysa tests, Reysa downspout test).
- **Paint:** Reysa used flat high-temperature black spray; in a year-long USDA test, flat black held up while lacquer peeled off the metal (FPL collector). A filmy coating appeared inside the glazing of Reysa's pop can collector; he thought paint outgassing might be the cause but wasn't sure, and it didn't hurt output (Reysa pop can test). The USDA test saw no deposit on its glazing from the wood but couldn't rule one out where wood runs hotter (FPL collector). Let paint cure in the sun before you close the box.

## Heat, wood and plastic

A collector with no air moving through it (a stalled fan, closed vents, summer) gets far hotter than one that's running. In a year-long USDA test of homemade wood-framed collectors left sealed, insulated boxes passed 93 °C (200 °F) for about 4 hours a day in April, and one did so on 123 days of the year (FPL collector).
- Wood heated near 100 °C (212 °F) for months has caught fire on its own in field reports, so USDA treats 100 °C as the limit for long exposure, and strength drops long before that (FPL collector). Keep wood, paper, cloth and foam from touching the absorber; use metal brackets and an air gap.
- Extruded polystyrene foam is rated only to about 71 °C (160 °F) by its maker and warped badly above 93 °C (FPL collector). Use fibreglass or mineral wool behind the absorber: the USDA authors advise another insulation type wherever stagnation is expected even briefly (FPL collector). Foam boards are combustible plastic, so keep them away from the absorber and anything else that gets hot.
- Condensation inside the box stained the plywood backs (FPL collector): seal the inside and give it a small drain hole at the bottom.
- The glazing has limits too. Palram rates its polycarbonate to +100 °C for long exposure and +120 °C for short spells, and warns that dark objects and metal in contact with the sheet can collect heat and damage it (Palram guide). A stalled box passed 93 °C in the USDA test (FPL collector), so keep an air gap between absorber and glazing. One of the glass sheets in that test cracked (FPL collector).
- Don't leave it stalled for long. If you won't use it for weeks, cover the glazing.

## Night: dampers

Warm room air flowing back through a cold collector cools the room. A wall panel needs a light one-way backdraft damper so it can't run in reverse when the sun isn't on it (Kornher handbook). A simple one: thin plastic film hung over the opening on the side the air flows towards, so the flow pushes it open and it drops shut when the flow reverses. A hinged board you close at dusk does the same job. A window box collector is self-damping at night and needs no damper (Kornher handbook). It works best on a window at least 1.2 m (4 ft) above the ground (Kornher handbook).

## Fan or no fan

- A fan wired straight to its own small solar panel runs only when the sun shines, so it needs no thermostat, and the harder the sun, the faster it runs.
- Reysa ran about 2.3–3.4 cfm per square foot of collector, roughly 12–17 L/s per m² (Reysa screen test, Reysa pop can test). Higher flow keeps the collector cooler, so it loses less heat through the glazing (Kornher handbook).
- Check the panel's open-circuit volts against the fan's rating first: a 12 V panel can read about 20 V with nothing connected ([Test a solar panel](#guides/test_solar_panel)). Wiring: [DC wiring](#guides/skill_dc_wiring).

## Glazing

- **Polycarbonate twinwall** (greenhouse and carport panels): clear 4–10 mm sheet lets through about 79–82% of the light, and standard sheet has UV protection on one side only (Palram Sunlite): that side faces the sun.
- **Glass:** storm windows, patio and shower doors. Tempered glass can't be cut; size the box to the pane.

## Don't block your way out

A window box takes up a window. Never use the only window in a sleeping room that opens, and never block the exit window of the warm room: see [Staying warm](#guides/skill_staying_warm).
